# Why Writing Is Different {background-color="#530153"}

## The paper is where the thinking happens

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card .line}
[Yesterday: implementation]{.ct}

Code · tables · charts · slides

<span class="muted">Check it by **running** it.</span>
:::

::: {.card .dark}
[Today: the paper]{.ct}

What the estimates **mean** · which claim they carry · what to leave out

Check it by **thinking**. There is nothing to run.
:::
:::

::: {.punch}
Your name is on it. You vouch for every sentence, including the agent's.
:::

::: {.notes}
Writing is not typing up results: it is where you decide what the evidence means, which caveats it needs, and what to leave out. If the agent writes the argument, the agent made the decisions the paper exists to make.
Journals already say this: AI cannot be an author, and authors are solely accountable for what it produced (AEA policy, covered in the Day 1 ethics session).
:::

## Human in the loop vs AI in the loop

```{=html}
<div class="flow-label">Human in the loop</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="step ai">AI drafts</div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step ai">AI polishes</div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you">You approve</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-label">AI in the loop</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="step you">You state the claim</div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you">You write the brief</div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step ai">AI drafts or comments</div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you">You decide</div>
</div>
<div class="key"><span class="you">you</span><span class="ai">agent</span></div>
```

::: {.punch}
Judgement **before** the draft, not only after it.
:::

::: {.notes}
In the first row your judgement arrives after the thinking is done: you are reviewing someone else's argument. In the second, the agent works inside decisions you already made, and you still rule on what it produces.
:::

## Why approving a finished draft fails

::: {.cards .c4}
::: {.card .big-ic}
<svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg>

[Fluent feels right]{.ct}

Polished prose invites a yes
:::

::: {.card .big-ic}
<svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M2 12s3-7 10-7 10 7 10 7-3 7-10 7S2 12 2 12Z"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="3"/></svg>

[Reading ≠ deciding]{.ct}

You stop seeing what is missing
:::

::: {.card .big-ic}
<svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M3 12h4l3 8 4-16 3 8h4"/></svg>

[Voice drifts]{.ct}

Twenty small edits later, it sounds like the model
:::

::: {.card .big-ic}
<svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M12 9v4M12 17h.01"/><path d="M10.3 3.9 1.8 18a2 2 0 0 0 1.7 3h17a2 2 0 0 0 1.7-3L13.7 3.9a2 2 0 0 0-3.4 0Z"/></svg>

[Errors hide]{.ct}

In sentences that read well
:::
:::

::: {.punch}
A wrong table looks wrong. A wrong paragraph looks finished.
:::

::: {.notes}
Fluent text reads as correct, so checking slides into skimming. Approving an argument is easier than building one, so you stop noticing what is missing. Each accepted edit is small, but they add up to a paper in someone else's voice.
Line to land: this is why the workflow starts by interviewing you, and ends with you ruling on every comment and every change.
The demo draft used in the hands-on has 12 planted errors of exactly these kinds: a wrong number (5.2 vs 4.2 in the table), an invented dropout result, a fabricated citation, an overclaim with no cost data, and AI prose ("delve" three times). Each is caught by one specific check. Full list in INSTRUCTOR-seeded-defects.md.
:::

::: {.punch}
Four of the five steps are yours.

## Three skills

::: {.cards .c3}
::: {.card .dark .big-ic}
<svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M21 15a2 2 0 0 1-2 2H7l-4 4V5a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h14a2 2 0 0 1 2 2z"/></svg>

[setup]{.ct}

Interviews you

<span class="foot">→ `profile.md` + guides</span>
:::

::: {.card .big-ic}
<svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M12 20h9"/><path d="M16.5 3.5a2.12 2.12 0 0 1 3 3L7 19l-4 1 1-4Z"/></svg>

[write]{.ct}

Drafts one section at a time

<span class="foot">→ the paper, after you see the change</span>
:::

::: {.card .big-ic}
<svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><circle cx="11" cy="11" r="8"/><path d="m21 21-4.3-4.3"/></svg>

[review]{.ct}

Comments against the guides

<span class="foot">→ comment files, never the paper</span>
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
Baselines: econ-writing-skill and econ-paper-review-skill by Lu Han (github.com/hanlulong). They hold the general rules of good economics writing and refereeing. The WB skills add the author's preferences, the grounding in the project's own tables, and the approval steps.
:::

## Setup: the agent interviews you

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
```{=html}
<div class="chat">
  <div class="bubble agent"><span class="who">Agent</span>In one sentence, what is the main finding?</div>
  <div class="bubble me"><span class="who">You</span>Free school meals raised attendance by about 4 points, most for girls and rural schools.</div>
  <div class="bubble agent"><span class="who">Agent</span>What do you fear a referee will say?</div>
  <div class="bubble me"><span class="who">You</span>That parallel trends is untested.</div>
  <div class="bubble agent"><span class="who">Agent</span>Anything you want in every draft?</div>
  <div class="bubble me"><span class="who">You</span>The number on page one.</div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
```{=html}
<div class="card dark" style="margin-top:1.2em">
  <h4>profile.md</h4>
  <div>✓ claim, <b>in your words</b></div>
  <div>✓ your biggest fear</div>
  <div>✓ your conventions</div>
  <div class="foot">~10–15 min</div>
</div>
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Answers taken from the demo's pre-baked profile. The agent also asks who the paper is for, which papers you admire or dislike, and for outlet rules and old referee reports. The main finding is always typed by the author: the agent may sharpen it, never invent it.
:::

## Before the interview: four folders

::: {.cards .c4}
::: {.card .dark}
[`positive/`]{.ct}

Papers you admire

<span class="ex">A PRWP with an intro you like</span>

<span class="foot">Setup asks: what is it great **for**?</span>
:::

::: {.card}
[`negative/`]{.ct}

Writing you dislike

<span class="ex">A paper that buries its result on page 9</span>

<span class="foot">Setup asks: what puts you off, **exactly**?</span>
:::

::: {.card}
[`guidelines/`]{.ct}

Rules of the target outlet

<span class="ex">PRWP author note · journal guide · a report template</span>

<span class="foot">Setup asks: **binding** or aspirational?</span>
:::

::: {.card}
[`feedback/`]{.ct}

Old referee reports, seminar notes

<span class="ex">The report on your last paper</span>

<span class="foot">Setup asks: which were **fair**?</span>
:::
:::

::: {.punch}
PDF, Markdown or text. Empty folders are fine.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is `wb-paper/references/`. Setup creates the four folders and asks you to drop files in before the questions start. The interview then walks them folder by folder, one file per question. Each folder has one question that matters: what a good paper is good for, scopes what gets copied from it; the exact dislike turns into a "never" rule; bindingness decides whether a guideline is a hard check or a style to lean toward; the fairness call on old criticism decides whether the draft must comply with it or merely preempt the misreading.
An empty folder costs one line ("no outlet rules, I'll use PRWP defaults") and the skill falls back to the baseline. Files you add later are picked up when you rerun setup.
:::

## What setup does with them

```{=html}
<style>
.xt { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1.1fr 2fr 1.7fr; gap: 6px 14px; font-size: 0.72em; line-height: 1.3; margin-top: 0.5em; align-items: stretch; }
.xt .h { font-family: "Montserrat", sans-serif; font-weight: 700; color: var(--navy); font-size: 0.95em; padding: 0 6px 4px; border-bottom: 2px solid var(--cyan); }
.xt .f { background: var(--blue); color: #fff; border-radius: 8px; padding: 10px 12px; font-family: "Fira Code", monospace; font-size: 0.95em; display: flex; align-items: center; }
.xt .e, .xt .u { background: var(--pale); color: var(--navy); border-radius: 8px; padding: 10px 12px; }
.xt .e i { display: block; font-style: italic; opacity: 0.85; margin-top: 3px; font-size: 0.95em; }
.reveal .xt .e code { font-size: 0.9em; }
</style>
<div class="xt">
  <div class="h">You drop in</div><div class="h">Setup extracts</div><div class="h">Then: drafting follows · comments check</div>
  <div class="f">positive/</div>
  <div class="e">Craft patterns, not text<i>"each intro paragraph opens with a claim sentence; evidence follows"</i></div>
  <div class="u">A convention the draft follows and a comment pass can mark pass/fail</div>
  <div class="f">negative/</div>
  <div class="e">A "never" rule<i>"never three pages before the first number"</i></div>
  <div class="u">Same. Often the most useful entries</div>
  <div class="f">guidelines/</div>
  <div class="e">Binding constraints<i>abstract ≤ 150 words · disclaimer footnote · AI-disclosure policy</i></div>
  <div class="u">Hard checks. Outrank the baseline and your own preferences</div>
  <div class="f">feedback/</div>
  <div class="e">Recurring criticisms, fair vs misread<i>"generalises far beyond its setting"</i></div>
  <div class="u">Top priority in the guides. Optional guide: <b>The Referee You Keep Getting</b></div>
</div>
```

::: {.punch}
Every entry names its source and how to check it.
:::

::: {.notes}
The unit of extraction is a convention entry: an imperative rule, a one-pass check, a quoted fragment of at most 25 words as evidence, and the sections it applies to. Three tests: could the drafting skill follow it without asking, could the review skill mark pass/fail without a judgement call, and does it point at a specific passage. "The intro flows well" fails all three.
Two more rules. Delta: anything the baseline already enforces is not recorded again; if your materials show it matters unusually much to you, it becomes a priority pointer instead. Imitation boundary: the skill extracts how a paper is built, never its sentences.
Referee reports are the highest-signal source: criticism you received predicts criticism to come. Identities and the outlet's decision are stripped; only the content is used. Fair criticism becomes a compliance check, a misreading becomes a defensibility check (does the draft preempt it).
:::

## Every AI action is on the record

```{=html}
<div class="flow" style="margin-top:0.6em;align-items:center">
  <div class="tree" style="flex:2;white-space:normal"><b>wb-paper/log.md</b><br>10:31 · setup · interview<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;offered: A lean | B full → <b>you chose B</b><br>11:02 · review · accuracy · Results<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;3 comments → <b>2 accepted, 1 challenged</b></div>
  <span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you" style="flex:1"><svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M14 2H6a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v16a2 2 0 0 0 2 2h12a2 2 0 0 0 2-2V8z"/><path d="M14 2v6h6M9 15l2 2 4-4"/></svg><b>AI-use disclosure</b><small>generated at submission</small></div>
</div>
```

::: {.punch}
The log is what the disclosure statement is written from.
:::

::: {.notes}
The log records what the agent was given, the options it offered and what you chose. Each AI change is also saved separately from your own edits, so you can see and undo it. The first entry is from the demo log; the second is illustrative.
:::

# Hands-on: Draft or Comment {background-color="#530153"}

## Pick a task and a project

```{=html}
<div class="flow-label">1 · What do you want to do?</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="step you"><svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><circle cx="11" cy="11" r="8"/><path d="m21 21-4.3-4.3"/></svg><b>Comment</b><small>needs a draft</small></div>
  <div class="step you"><svg class="ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M12 20h9"/><path d="M16.5 3.5a2.12 2.12 0 0 1 3 3L7 19l-4 1 1-4Z"/></svg><b>Draft</b><small>needs tables and notes</small></div>
</div>
<div class="flow-label">2 · Which project?</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="step ai"><b>Demo · with draft</b><small><code>zambia-attendance-with-draft/</code><br>12 planted errors, guides set up</small></div>
  <div class="step ai"><b>Demo · no draft</b><small><code>zambia-attendance-no-draft/</code><br>tables + concept note, no paper</small></div>
  <div class="step ai"><b>Your own paper</b><small>Quarto, LaTeX or Markdown<br>+ <code>skills.zip</code></small></div>
</div>
```

::: {.punch}
Any combination works. Setup asks what you want to do.
:::

::: {.notes}
Both demo folders are the same fictional study: school meals and attendance in Zambia, 1,840 schools, 2021–2023. The natural pairings are comment on the with-draft demo and draft on the no-draft demo, but nothing prevents drafting a new section in the with-draft project or commenting on a section you just drafted in the no-draft project. On your own paper you can do either, or both, in the same folder: a comment pass on what exists, then draft the missing section.
Only one real constraint: comments need a draft. If there is none, setup says so and offers drafting.
:::

## Flow A · Comment

```{=html}
<div class="flow" style="margin-top:0.4em">
  <div class="step ai"><b>1 · Open</b><small>the project folder in VS Code</small></div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you"><b>2 · Paste</b><small>the first message</small></div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you"><b>3 · Pick the scope</b><small>guide × domain × section</small></div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you"><b>4 · Triage</b><small>accept · reject · challenge · defer</small></div>
</div>
<div class="flow-label">Demo (guides already set up)</div>
<div class="prompt">Follow skills/wb-paper-review/SKILL.md. Scope: Methodologist · accuracy · Results.</div>
<div class="flow-label">Your own draft (no guides yet)</div>
<div class="prompt">Follow skills/wb-paper-setup/SKILL.md on the Quick route. I am the author. I want comments on my draft.</div>
```

::: {.callout-note-custom}
On your own paper, setup runs first (~10–15 min), then hands off to comments. Point it at your draft and your tables when asked.
:::

::: {.notes}
The with-draft demo ships profile and guides, so review starts immediately. On a participant's own draft the review skill needs a profile and will offer setup; starting with setup saves a round trip. The scope question is the same either way: pick one guide, one domain, one section. Accuracy on Results is the fastest first pass because every comment can be checked against a table.
:::

## Flow B · Draft

```{=html}
<div class="flow" style="margin-top:0.4em">
  <div class="step ai"><b>1 · Open</b><small>the project folder in VS Code</small></div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you"><b>2 · Paste</b><small>the first message</small></div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you"><b>3 · Interview</b><small>claim, fear, conventions · ~10 min</small></div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you"><b>4 · Outline → bullets → prose</b><small>you approve each step</small></div>
</div>
<div class="flow-label">Demo (no draft) and your own project</div>
<div class="prompt">Follow skills/wb-paper-setup/SKILL.md on the Quick route. I am the author. I want to draft the Results section.</div>
```

::: {.callout-note-custom}
Already have a draft? Drafting still works: ask for a missing section, or **Rewrite** mode on a paragraph you wrote. Numbers come from your tables only.
:::

::: {.notes}
Same first message for the demo and for a participant's own project: setup, then it offers drafting. On their own paper the interview asks where the tables are (grounding pointers) and the agent will not write a number it cannot find there; everything else becomes an [AUTHOR:] marker.
If they already have a full draft, suggest Results or a section they have been putting off, or Rewrite mode on an existing paragraph: meaning preserved, voice kept, before/after shown.
:::

## Set up

```{=html}
<div class="flow" style="margin-top:0.4em">
  <div class="step ai"><b>Demo</b><small>unzip the .zip → open that folder</small></div>
  <div class="step ai"><b>Your paper</b><small>unzip <code>skills.zip</code> into your paper folder → open that folder</small></div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="tree" style="margin-top:0.6em">your-paper/
├── skills/            <em>← from skills.zip</em>
├── paper/             <em>your draft, if any</em>
├── outputs/           <em>your tables and figures</em>
└── wb-paper/references/   <em>created by setup, empty is fine</em>
    ├── positive/      <em>papers you admire</em>
    ├── negative/      <em>writing you dislike</em>
    ├── guidelines/    <em>outlet rules</em>
    └── feedback/      <em>old referee reports</em></div>
```

::: {.notes}
Most common issue: opening a file instead of the folder. Each demo zip already contains skills/; if the agent cannot find SKILL.md, the folder opened is probably one level too high or too low. Folder names in your own project do not have to match: setup asks where the draft and the tables are.
Word files: the agent edits .docx badly. Convert with pandoc first and render back to Word at the end.
:::

## What to watch for

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card}
[A · Comment]{.ct}

☐ Demo: catches **5.2 vs 4.2**? The dropout claim?<br>
☐ Every comment points at a table or a sentence?<br>
☐ Challenge one: upheld or withdrawn, with reasons?
:::

::: {.card}
[B · Draft]{.ct}

☐ Asks before it writes?<br>
☐ Every number in your `outputs/`?<br>
☐ Where are the `[AUTHOR:]` markers?
:::
:::

::: {.punch}
After each step, open `wb-paper/log.md`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Demo comment track, if time: run Methodologist · design · full draft. It should put the parallel-trends problem first, because that is the author's fear in the profile. Draft track: read each change before accepting it.
On their own paper the checks are the same minus the planted errors: does each comment quote the draft and name the table, and does the draft refuse to invent numbers.
:::

## Only for Working Papers?

::: {.cards .c3 style="font-size:0.85em"}
::: {.card .dark}
[Working papers · journal articles]{.ct}

The default. The baseline is economics writing: structure, claims, exhibits, identification.

<span class="foot">PRWP defaults if you add nothing</span>
:::

::: {.card}
[Reports · policy notes · briefs]{.ct}

Yes. Tell setup the outlet and put its rules in `guidelines/`. Length limits, required sections and audience become checks.

<span class="foot">Policy guide + `outlet` checks</span>
:::

::: {.card .line}
[What stays the same]{.ct}

Numbers only from your tables · claims checked against your evidence · you triage every comment · everything logged

:::
:::

::: {.punch}
The guides are text files. Edit them if the defaults do not fit.
:::

::: {.notes}
This question will come up. The honest answer: the skills were built around working papers, and the vendored baseline (econ-write) is economics-paper craft, so a report or a policy note gets some advice that does not apply, such as intro structure or the 35–45 page target. Setup handles the difference in three places: the target-outlet question, the guidelines/ folder (a report template or a GP's style rules become binding outlet constraints), and the policy guide, whose brief is audience and how far the recommendations may go. The grounding and triage rules do not depend on the output type at all.
What it is not for: Word-native workflows (convert first) and outputs with no underlying tables, where there is nothing to ground the numbers in.
:::

## Use it after today

1. Drop in what you have. Empty is fine.
2. Run setup once. Edit the guides.
3. Before the next draft goes to a coauthor: **one** comment pass, triaged by you.

::: {.notes}
Setup creates the four reference folders if they are missing and asks you to add files; empty folders fall back to defaults. Work in Quarto, LaTeX or Markdown while the agent is involved and render to Word at the end if someone needs it.
:::
